OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $f(N)$ be the size of the largest subset $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that every $n\in A+A$ is squarefree. Estimate $f(N)$. In particular, is it true that $f(N)\leq N^{o(1)}$, or even $f(N) \leq (\log N)^{O(1)}$?
#1109: [ErSa87]
number theory
First studied by Erdős and Sárközy [ErSa87], who proved\[\log N \ll f(N) \ll N^{3/4}\log N,\]and guessed the lower bound is nearer the truth. Sárközy [Sa92c] extended this to consider the case of $A+B$ and also looking for sumsets which are $k$-power-free.
Gyarmati [Gy01] gave an alternative proof of $f(N)\gg \log N$, and also gave new bounds for the case of $A+B$. Konyagin [Ko04] improved this to\[ \log\log N(\log N)^2\ll f(N) \ll N^{11/15+o(1)}.\]The infinite analogue of this problem is [1103]. (In particular upper bounds for this $f(N)$ directly imply lower bounds for the size of the $a_j$ considered there.)

 I computed $f(N)$ for $1 \le N \le 250$.
Method: The vertices are odd squarefree integers $a \le N$ (even or non-squarefree $a$ fail since $2a$ is not squarefree), with an edge between distinct $a,b$ if $a+b$ is not squarefree. Then $f(N)$ is the maximum independent set size. I used branch-and-bound with bitsets, cross-checked against brute-force for small $N$.
$$\begin{aligned}
 1 &\le N \le 4 &:\qquad f(N) &= 1\\
 5 &\le N \le 18 &:\qquad f(N) &= 2\\
 19 &\le N \le 22 &:\qquad f(N) &= 3\\
 23 &\le N \le 36 &:\qquad f(N) &= 4\\
 37 &\le N \le 40 &:\qquad f(N) &= 5\\
 41 &\le N \le 58 &:\qquad f(N) &= 6\\
 59 &\le N \le 86 &:\qquad f(N) &= 7\\
 87 &\le N \le 100 &:\qquad f(N) &= 8\\
101 &\le N \le 104 &:\qquad f(N) &= 9\\
105 &\le N \le 112 &:\qquad f(N) &= 10\\
113 &\le N \le 130 &:\qquad f(N) &= 11\\
131 &\le N \le 150 &:\qquad f(N) &= 12\\
151 &\le N \le 158 &:\qquad f(N) &= 13\\
159 &\le N \le 166 &:\qquad f(N) &= 14\\
167 &\le N \le 194 &:\qquad f(N) &= 15\\
195 &\le N \le 202 &:\qquad f(N) &= 16\\
203 &\le N \le 238 &:\qquad f(N) &= 17\\
239 &\le N \le 250 &:\qquad f(N) &= 18
\end{aligned}$$
Example: $f(101) = 9$ is achieved by $\{5, 17, 29, 41, 53, 65, 77, 89, 101\}$, an arithmetic progression with common difference 12. All pairwise sums have the form $10 + 12k$, which is squarefree for $k \le 16$.
The sequence of transition points $(1, 5, 19, 23, 37, 41, 59, 87, 101, 105, 113, 131, 151, 159, 167, 195, 203, 239, \ldots)$ does not appear in OEIS.
